case_info.scenario: A 2-month-old boy, born at 39 weeks 1 day of gestation via normal spontaneous vaginal delivery with normal newborn screening results presented with a 10-day history of rash. On presentation, his temperature was 37.0 °C (98.6 °F); blood pressure, 113/74 mm Hg; and heart rate, 132 beats/min. Skin examination showed multiple annular, pink papules and plaques with hyperpigmentation and desquamation on the scalp, palms, and soles (Figure 1). Physical examination showed hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory testing revealed elevated levels of aspartate aminotransferase (238 U/L [reference, 9-80 U/L]) (3.97 μkat/L [reference, 0.15-1.34 μkat/L]) and alanine aminotransferase (261 U/L [reference, 13-45 U/L]) (4.36 μkat/L [reference, 0.22-0.75 μkat/L). Results of testing for antinuclear antibody, anti-SSA, and anti-SSB were negative. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed hepatosplenomegaly. Of note, his mother had a negative rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test at 12 and 32 weeks of pregnancy and a negative HIV test at 12 weeks of pregnancy.

case_info.caption: Multiple annular, pink papules and thin plaques with slight hyperpigmentation and desquamation on patient’s right arm, forearm, and palm.
case_info.explanation: C. Perform RPR andTreponema pallidumparticle agglutination (TPPA) testing in the infant and mother. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that characteristic rash on the palms, soles, and scalp, along with transaminitis and hepatosplenomegaly on physical examination and ultrasound, are consistent with congenital syphilis. Topical corticosteroids (choice A) are not appropriate treatment for undiagnosed rash in an infant. Skin biopsy (choice B) is invasive and not the preferred initial option. Transaminitis and hepatomegaly with rash are not characteristic of superficial fungal infection, so KOH preparation (choice D) is not indicated. Congenital syphilis, caused by the spirocheteT pallidum,is transmitted to the fetus through the placenta or through direct contact with lesions during delivery.1Cases of congenital syphilis in the US exceeded 3800 in 2023, a more than 10-fold increase over the prior decade.2Risk factors for congenital syphilis include inadequate prenatal care, younger maternal age, lower educational attainment, low family income, unstable housing, substance use disorder, and history of incarceration.3The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends screening all pregnant women for syphilis at their first prenatal visit and in the third trimester, with risk-based screening at the time of delivery. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends universal testing 3 times in pregnancy.4-6All pregnant patients who test positive for syphilis should be treated immediately to decrease the risk of congenital syphilis.5,6 Approximately 55% of neonates with congenital syphilis are asymptomatic at birth; 31% of symptomatic cases are diagnosed after age 3 months.7Infants with early congenital syphilis (onset before age 2 years) may have bullous or mucocutaneous eruptions (40%), hepatobiliary dysfunction (33%-100%), anemia and thrombocytopenia (37%), and osteochondritis or periostitis on skeletal radiography (75%).8The classic skin rash (oval, copper-red macular or papular, often desquamating, lesions on the palms and soles or elsewhere on the body) is contagious due to presence of spirochetes in the lesions.9Up to 60% of symptomatic newborns develop neurosyphilis, which may present with seizures and/or cranial nerve palsies.8Approximately 40% of infants born to pregnant patients with untreated syphilis develop late congenital syphilis (onset after age 2 years), which may present with bony abnormalities (osteochondritis or periostitis), Hutchinson teeth (notched, widely spaced teeth), ocular abnormalities (interstitial keratitis, uveitis, chorioretinitis), and sensorineural hearing loss.8,9 The CDC stratifies patients with possible congenital syphilis into 4 categories: confirmed or highly probable, possible, less likely, and unlikely based on characteristic clinical findings and nontreponemal test results.5Because maternal nontreponemal antibodies passively cross the placenta, diagnosis of early congenital syphilis requires nontreponemal testing (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory [VDRL] or RPR) of the infant and mother, using the same assay. An infant titer of 4 or greater times the maternal titer confirms congenital syphilis.8,9Infants with physical findings (eg, characteristic rash) or an RPR titer more than 4-fold higher than the maternal titer should undergo testing with complete blood cell count, liver function tests, lumbar puncture and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, and long-bone radiographs.5 The differential diagnosis of congenital syphilis includes impetigo, fungal infection, neonatal lupus erythematosus, and SCORTCH infections (syphilis, cytomegalovirus, other viruses [eg, HIV, hepatitis B, Zika, parvovirus, rubella, toxoplasmosis, chickenpox, herpes simplex]).10 For confirmed or highly probable cases of congenital syphilis, standard therapy consists of a 10-day course of intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G.5After treatment, neonates with congenital syphilis should undergo regular monitoring of symptoms and serologic testing every 3 months until their titers decline at least 4-fold from the peak titer.9 The infant’s RPR was reactive, with a titer of 1:2048 (8-fold higher than maternal RPR [1:256]). The infant’s TPPA test result was positive. Results of HIV testing of the infant and mother were negative. Skeletal radiographs showed metaphyseal destruction on the medial aspects of the bilateral proximal tibias (Figure 2). CSF analysis showed a leukocyte count of 23 cells/μL (reference, 0-20 cells/μL), protein level of 170.9 mg/dL (reference, 15-45 mg/dL), and a reactive VDRL (titer 1:8), consistent with neurosyphilis. Findings on cerebral ultrasound, ocular examination, and hearing assessment were normal. The patient received 50 000 IU/kg of aqueous crystalline penicillin G every 6 hours for 10 days. At 6-week follow up, the infant’s skin lesions had resolved, liver function test results normalized, and the bony radiographic abnormalities had resolved. No clinical sequelae such as hearing loss, visual disturbances, or developmental delays were observed. At 9-month follow-up, the infant’s RPR titer had decreased more than 4-fold, to 1:16.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: C. Perform RPR andTreponema pallidumparticle agglutination (TPPA) testing in the infant and mother. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that characteristic rash on the palms, soles, and scalp, along with transaminitis and hepatosplenomegaly on physical examination and ultrasound, are consistent with congenital syphilis. Topical corticosteroids (choice A) are not appropriate treatment for undiagnosed rash in an infant. Skin biopsy (choice B) is invasive and not the preferred initial option. Transaminitis and hepatomegaly with rash are not characteristic of superficial fungal infection, so KOH preparation (choice D) is not indicated. Congenital syphilis, caused by the spirocheteT pallidum,is transmitted to the fetus through the placenta or through direct contact with lesions during delivery.1Cases of congenital syphilis in the US exceeded 3800 in 2023, a more than 10-fold increase over the prior decade.2Risk factors for congenital syphilis include inadequate prenatal care, younger maternal age, lower educational attainment, low family income, unstable housing, substance use disorder, and history of incarceration.3The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends screening all pregnant women for syphilis at their first prenatal visit and in the third trimester, with risk-based screening at the time of delivery. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends universal testing 3 times in pregnancy.4-6All pregnant patients who test positive for syphilis should be treated immediately to decrease the risk of congenital syphilis.5,6 Approximately 55% of neonates with congenital syphilis are asymptomatic at birth; 31% of symptomatic cases are diagnosed after age 3 months.7Infants with early congenital syphilis (onset before age 2 years) may have bullous or mucocutaneous eruptions (40%), hepatobiliary dysfunction (33%-100%), anemia and thrombocytopenia (37%), and osteochondritis or periostitis on skeletal radiography (75%).8The classic skin rash (oval, copper-red macular or papular, often desquamating, lesions on the palms and soles or elsewhere on the body) is contagious due to presence of spirochetes in the lesions.9Up to 60% of symptomatic newborns develop neurosyphilis, which may present with seizures and/or cranial nerve palsies.8Approximately 40% of infants born to pregnant patients with untreated syphilis develop late congenital syphilis (onset after age 2 years), which may present with bony abnormalities (osteochondritis or periostitis), Hutchinson teeth (notched, widely spaced teeth), ocular abnormalities (interstitial keratitis, uveitis, chorioretinitis), and sensorineural hearing loss.8,9 The CDC stratifies patients with possible congenital syphilis into 4 categories: confirmed or highly probable, possible, less likely, and unlikely based on characteristic clinical findings and nontreponemal test results.5Because maternal nontreponemal antibodies passively cross the placenta, diagnosis of early congenital syphilis requires nontreponemal testing (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory [VDRL] or RPR) of the infant and mother, using the same assay. An infant titer of 4 or greater times the maternal titer confirms congenital syphilis.8,9Infants with physical findings (eg, characteristic rash) or an RPR titer more than 4-fold higher than the maternal titer should undergo testing with complete blood cell count, liver function tests, lumbar puncture and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, and long-bone radiographs.5 The differential diagnosis of congenital syphilis includes impetigo, fungal infection, neonatal lupus erythematosus, and SCORTCH infections (syphilis, cytomegalovirus, other viruses [eg, HIV, hepatitis B, Zika, parvovirus, rubella, toxoplasmosis, chickenpox, herpes simplex]).10 For confirmed or highly probable cases of congenital syphilis, standard therapy consists of a 10-day course of intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G.5After treatment, neonates with congenital syphilis should undergo regular monitoring of symptoms and serologic testing every 3 months until their titers decline at least 4-fold from the peak titer.9 The infant’s RPR was reactive, with a titer of 1:2048 (8-fold higher than maternal RPR [1:256]). The infant’s TPPA test result was positive. Results of HIV testing of the infant and mother were negative. Skeletal radiographs showed metaphyseal destruction on the medial aspects of the bilateral proximal tibias (Figure 2). CSF analysis showed a leukocyte count of 23 cells/μL (reference, 0-20 cells/μL), protein level of 170.9 mg/dL (reference, 15-45 mg/dL), and a reactive VDRL (titer 1:8), consistent with neurosyphilis. Findings on cerebral ultrasound, ocular examination, and hearing assessment were normal. The patient received 50 000 IU/kg of aqueous crystalline penicillin G every 6 hours for 10 days. At 6-week follow up, the infant’s skin lesions had resolved, liver function test results normalized, and the bony radiographic abnormalities had resolved. No clinical sequelae such as hearing loss, visual disturbances, or developmental delays were observed. At 9-month follow-up, the infant’s RPR titer had decreased more than 4-fold, to 1:16.

case_info.explanation: C. Perform RPR andTreponema pallidumparticle agglutination (TPPA) testing in the infant and mother. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that characteristic rash on the palms, soles, and scalp, along with transaminitis and hepatosplenomegaly on physical examination and ultrasound, are consistent with congenital syphilis. Topical corticosteroids (choice A) are not appropriate treatment for undiagnosed rash in an infant. Skin biopsy (choice B) is invasive and not the preferred initial option. Transaminitis and hepatomegaly with rash are not characteristic of superficial fungal infection, so KOH preparation (choice D) is not indicated. Congenital syphilis, caused by the spirocheteT pallidum,is transmitted to the fetus through the placenta or through direct contact with lesions during delivery.1Cases of congenital syphilis in the US exceeded 3800 in 2023, a more than 10-fold increase over the prior decade.2Risk factors for congenital syphilis include inadequate prenatal care, younger maternal age, lower educational attainment, low family income, unstable housing, substance use disorder, and history of incarceration.3The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends screening all pregnant women for syphilis at their first prenatal visit and in the third trimester, with risk-based screening at the time of delivery. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends universal testing 3 times in pregnancy.4-6All pregnant patients who test positive for syphilis should be treated immediately to decrease the risk of congenital syphilis.5,6 Approximately 55% of neonates with congenital syphilis are asymptomatic at birth; 31% of symptomatic cases are diagnosed after age 3 months.7Infants with early congenital syphilis (onset before age 2 years) may have bullous or mucocutaneous eruptions (40%), hepatobiliary dysfunction (33%-100%), anemia and thrombocytopenia (37%), and osteochondritis or periostitis on skeletal radiography (75%).8The classic skin rash (oval, copper-red macular or papular, often desquamating, lesions on the palms and soles or elsewhere on the body) is contagious due to presence of spirochetes in the lesions.9Up to 60% of symptomatic newborns develop neurosyphilis, which may present with seizures and/or cranial nerve palsies.8Approximately 40% of infants born to pregnant patients with untreated syphilis develop late congenital syphilis (onset after age 2 years), which may present with bony abnormalities (osteochondritis or periostitis), Hutchinson teeth (notched, widely spaced teeth), ocular abnormalities (interstitial keratitis, uveitis, chorioretinitis), and sensorineural hearing loss.8,9 The CDC stratifies patients with possible congenital syphilis into 4 categories: confirmed or highly probable, possible, less likely, and unlikely based on characteristic clinical findings and nontreponemal test results.5Because maternal nontreponemal antibodies passively cross the placenta, diagnosis of early congenital syphilis requires nontreponemal testing (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory [VDRL] or RPR) of the infant and mother, using the same assay. An infant titer of 4 or greater times the maternal titer confirms congenital syphilis.8,9Infants with physical findings (eg, characteristic rash) or an RPR titer more than 4-fold higher than the maternal titer should undergo testing with complete blood cell count, liver function tests, lumbar puncture and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, and long-bone radiographs.5 The differential diagnosis of congenital syphilis includes impetigo, fungal infection, neonatal lupus erythematosus, and SCORTCH infections (syphilis, cytomegalovirus, other viruses [eg, HIV, hepatitis B, Zika, parvovirus, rubella, toxoplasmosis, chickenpox, herpes simplex]).10 For confirmed or highly probable cases of congenital syphilis, standard therapy consists of a 10-day course of intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G.5After treatment, neonates with congenital syphilis should undergo regular monitoring of symptoms and serologic testing every 3 months until their titers decline at least 4-fold from the peak titer.9 The infant’s RPR was reactive, with a titer of 1:2048 (8-fold higher than maternal RPR [1:256]). The infant’s TPPA test result was positive. Results of HIV testing of the infant and mother were negative. Skeletal radiographs showed metaphyseal destruction on the medial aspects of the bilateral proximal tibias (Figure 2). CSF analysis showed a leukocyte count of 23 cells/μL (reference, 0-20 cells/μL), protein level of 170.9 mg/dL (reference, 15-45 mg/dL), and a reactive VDRL (titer 1:8), consistent with neurosyphilis. Findings on cerebral ultrasound, ocular examination, and hearing assessment were normal. The patient received 50 000 IU/kg of aqueous crystalline penicillin G every 6 hours for 10 days. At 6-week follow up, the infant’s skin lesions had resolved, liver function test results normalized, and the bony radiographic abnormalities had resolved. No clinical sequelae such as hearing loss, visual disturbances, or developmental delays were observed. At 9-month follow-up, the infant’s RPR titer had decreased more than 4-fold, to 1:16.

case_info.explanation: C. Perform RPR andTreponema pallidumparticle agglutination (TPPA) testing in the infant and mother. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that characteristic rash on the palms, soles, and scalp, along with transaminitis and hepatosplenomegaly on physical examination and ultrasound, are consistent with congenital syphilis. Topical corticosteroids (choice A) are not appropriate treatment for undiagnosed rash in an infant. Skin biopsy (choice B) is invasive and not the preferred initial option. Transaminitis and hepatomegaly with rash are not characteristic of superficial fungal infection, so KOH preparation (choice D) is not indicated. Congenital syphilis, caused by the spirocheteT pallidum,is transmitted to the fetus through the placenta or through direct contact with lesions during delivery.1Cases of congenital syphilis in the US exceeded 3800 in 2023, a more than 10-fold increase over the prior decade.2Risk factors for congenital syphilis include inadequate prenatal care, younger maternal age, lower educational attainment, low family income, unstable housing, substance use disorder, and history of incarceration.3The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends screening all pregnant women for syphilis at their first prenatal visit and in the third trimester, with risk-based screening at the time of delivery. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends universal testing 3 times in pregnancy.4-6All pregnant patients who test positive for syphilis should be treated immediately to decrease the risk of congenital syphilis.5,6 Approximately 55% of neonates with congenital syphilis are asymptomatic at birth; 31% of symptomatic cases are diagnosed after age 3 months.7Infants with early congenital syphilis (onset before age 2 years) may have bullous or mucocutaneous eruptions (40%), hepatobiliary dysfunction (33%-100%), anemia and thrombocytopenia (37%), and osteochondritis or periostitis on skeletal radiography (75%).8The classic skin rash (oval, copper-red macular or papular, often desquamating, lesions on the palms and soles or elsewhere on the body) is contagious due to presence of spirochetes in the lesions.9Up to 60% of symptomatic newborns develop neurosyphilis, which may present with seizures and/or cranial nerve palsies.8Approximately 40% of infants born to pregnant patients with untreated syphilis develop late congenital syphilis (onset after age 2 years), which may present with bony abnormalities (osteochondritis or periostitis), Hutchinson teeth (notched, widely spaced teeth), ocular abnormalities (interstitial keratitis, uveitis, chorioretinitis), and sensorineural hearing loss.8,9 The CDC stratifies patients with possible congenital syphilis into 4 categories: confirmed or highly probable, possible, less likely, and unlikely based on characteristic clinical findings and nontreponemal test results.5Because maternal nontreponemal antibodies passively cross the placenta, diagnosis of early congenital syphilis requires nontreponemal testing (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory [VDRL] or RPR) of the infant and mother, using the same assay. 1. Mental Demand
   Definition:

case_info.explanation: C. Perform RPR andTreponema pallidumparticle agglutination (TPPA) testing in the infant and mother. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that characteristic rash on the palms, soles, and scalp, along with transaminitis and hepatosplenomegaly on physical examination and ultrasound, are consistent with congenital syphilis. Topical corticosteroids (choice A) are not appropriate treatment for undiagnosed rash in an infant. Skin biopsy (choice B) is invasive and not the preferred initial option. Transaminitis and hepatomegaly with rash are not characteristic of superficial fungal infection, so KOH preparation (choice D) is not indicated. Congenital syphilis, caused by the spirocheteT pallidum,is transmitted to the fetus through the placenta or through direct contact with lesions during delivery.1Cases of congenital syphilis in the US exceeded 3800 in 2023, a more than 10-fold increase over the prior decade.2Risk factors for congenital syphilis include inadequate prenatal care, younger maternal age, lower educational attainment, low family income, unstable housing, substance use disorder, and history of incarceration.3The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends screening all pregnant women for syphilis at their first prenatal visit and in the third trimester, with risk-based screening at the time of delivery. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends universal testing 3 times in pregnancy.4-6All pregnant patients who test positive for syphilis should be treated immediately to decrease the risk of congenital syphilis.5,6 Approximately 55% of neonates with congenital syphilis are asymptomatic at birth; 31% of symptomatic cases are diagnosed after age 3 months.7Infants with early congenital syphilis (onset before age 2 years) may have bullous or mucocutaneous eruptions (40%), hepatobiliary dysfunction (33%-100%), anemia and thrombocytopenia (37%), and osteochondritis or periostitis on skeletal radiography (75%).8The classic skin rash (oval, copper-red macular or papular, often desquamating, lesions on the palms and soles or elsewhere on the body) is contagious due to presence of spirochetes in the lesions.9Up to 60% of symptomatic newborns develop neurosyphilis, which may present with seizures and/or cranial nerve palsies.8Approximately 40% of infants born to pregnant patients with untreated syphilis develop late congenital syphilis (onset after age 2 years), which may present with bony abnormalities (osteochondritis or periostitis), Hutchinson teeth (notched, widely spaced teeth), ocular abnormalities (interstitial keratitis, uveitis, chorioretinitis), and sensorineural hearing loss.8,9 The CDC stratifies patients with possible congenital syphilis into 4 categories: confirmed or highly probable, possible, less likely, and unlikely based on characteristic clinical findings and nontreponemal test results.5Because maternal nontreponemal antibodies passively cross the placenta, diagnosis of early congenital syphilis requires nontreponemal testing (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory [VDRL] or RPR) of the infant and mother, using the same assay. An infant titer of 4 or greater times the maternal titer confirms congenital syphilis.8,9Infants with physical findings (eg, characteristic rash) or an RPR titer more than 4-fold higher than the maternal titer should undergo testing with complete blood cell count, liver function tests, lumbar puncture and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, and long-bone radiographs.5 The differential diagnosis of congenital syphilis includes impetigo, fungal infection, neonatal lupus erythematosus, and SCORTCH infections (syphilis, cytomegalovirus, other viruses [eg, HIV, hepatitis B, Zika, parvovirus, rubella, toxoplasmosis, chickenpox, herpes simplex]).10 For confirmed or highly probable cases of congenital syphilis, standard therapy consists of a 10-day course of intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G.5After treatment, neonates with congenital syphilis should undergo regular monitoring of symptoms and serologic testing every 3 months until their titers decline at least 4-fold from the peak titer.9 The infant’s RPR was reactive, with a titer of 1:2048 (8-fold higher than maternal RPR [1:256]). The infant’s TPPA test result was positive. Results of HIV testing of the infant and mother were negative. Skeletal radiographs showed metaphyseal destruction on the medial aspects of the bilateral proximal tibias (Figure 2). CSF analysis showed a leukocyte count of 23 cells/μL (reference, 0-20 cells/μL), protein level of 170.9 mg/dL (reference, 15-45 mg/dL), and a reactive VDRL (titer 1:8), consistent with neurosyphilis. Findings on cerebral ultrasound, ocular examination, and hearing assessment were normal. The patient received 50 000 IU/kg of aqueous crystalline penicillin G every 6 hours for 10 days. At 6-week follow up, the infant’s skin lesions had resolved, liver function test results normalized, and the bony radiographic abnormalities had resolved. No clinical sequelae such as hearing loss, visual disturbances, or developmental delays were observed. At 9-month follow-up, the infant’s RPR titer had decreased more than 4-fold, to 1:16.

case_info.explanation: C. Perform RPR andTreponema pallidumparticle agglutination (TPPA) testing in the infant and mother. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that characteristic rash on the palms, soles, and scalp, along with transaminitis and hepatosplenomegaly on physical examination and ultrasound, are consistent with congenital syphilis. Topical corticosteroids (choice A) are not appropriate treatment for undiagnosed rash in an infant. Skin biopsy (choice B) is invasive and not the preferred initial option. Transaminitis and hepatomegaly with rash are not characteristic of superficial fungal infection, so KOH preparation (choice D) is not indicated. Congenital syphilis, caused by the spirocheteT pallidum,is transmitted to the fetus through the placenta or through direct contact with lesions during delivery.1Cases of congenital syphilis in the US exceeded 3800 in 2023, a more than 10-fold increase over the prior decade.2Risk factors for congenital syphilis include inadequate prenatal care, younger maternal age, lower educational attainment, low family income, unstable housing, substance use disorder, and history of incarceration.3The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends screening all pregnant women for syphilis at their first prenatal visit and in the third trimester, with risk-based screening at the time of delivery. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends universal testing 3 times in pregnancy.4-6All pregnant patients who test positive for syphilis should be treated immediately to decrease the risk of congenital syphilis.5,6 Approximately 55% of neonates with congenital syphilis are asymptomatic at birth; 31% of symptomatic cases are diagnosed after age 3 months.7Infants with early congenital syphilis (onset before age 2 years) may have bullous or mucocutaneous eruptions (40%), hepatobiliary dysfunction (33%-100%), anemia and thrombocytopenia (37%), and osteochondritis or periostitis on skeletal radiography (75%).8The classic skin rash (oval, copper-red macular or papular, often desquamating, lesions on the palms and soles or elsewhere on the body) is contagious due to presence of spirochetes in the lesions.9Up to 60% of symptomatic newborns develop neurosyphilis, which may present with seizures and/or cranial nerve palsies.8Approximately 40% of infants born to pregnant patients with untreated syphilis develop late congenital syphilis (onset after age 2 years), which may present with bony abnormalities (osteochondritis or periostitis), Hutchinson teeth (notched, widely spaced teeth), ocular abnormalities (interstitial keratitis, uveitis, chorioretinitis), and sensorineural hearing loss.8,9 The CDC stratifies patients with possible congenital syphilis into 4 categories: confirmed or highly probable, possible, less likely, and unlikely based on characteristic clinical findings and nontreponemal test results.5Because maternal nontreponemal antibodies passively cross the placenta, diagnosis of early congenital syphilis requires nontreponemal testing (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory [VDRL] or RPR) of the infant and mother, using the same assay. An infant titer of 4 or greater times the maternal titer confirms congenital syphilis.8,9Infants with physical findings (eg, characteristic rash) or an RPR titer more than 4-fold higher than the maternal titer should undergo testing with complete blood cell count, liver function tests, lumbar puncture and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, and long-bone radiographs.5 The differential diagnosis of congenital syphilis includes impetigo, fungal infection, neonatal lupus erythematosus, and SCORTCH infections (syphilis, cytomegalovirus, other viruses [eg, HIV, hepatitis B, Zika, parvovirus, rubella, toxoplasmosis, chickenpox, herpes simplex]).10 For confirmed or highly probable cases of congenital syphilis, standard therapy consists of a 10-day course of intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G.5After treatment, neonates with congenital syphilis should undergo regular monitoring of symptoms and serologic testing every 3 months until their titers decline at least 4-fold from the peak titer.9 The infant’s RPR was reactive, with a titer of 1:2048 (8-fold higher than maternal RPR [1:256]). The infant’s TPPA test result was positive. Results of HIV testing of the infant and mother were negative. Skeletal radiographs showed metaphyseal destruction on the medial aspects of the bilateral proximal tibias (Figure 2). CSF analysis showed a leukocyte count of 23 cells/μL (reference, 0-20 cells/μL), protein level of 170.9 mg/dL (reference, 15-45 mg/dL), and a reactive VDRL (titer 1:8), consistent with neurosyphilis. Findings on cerebral ultrasound, ocular examination, and hearing assessment were normal. The patient received 50 000 IU/kg of aqueous crystalline penicillin G every 6 hours for 10 days. At 6-week follow up, the infant’s skin lesions had resolved, liver function test results normalized, and the bony radiographic abnormalities had resolved. No clinical sequelae such as hearing loss, visual disturbances, or developmental delays were observed. At 9-month follow-up, the infant’s RPR titer had decreased more than 4-fold, to 1:16.

case_info.explanation: C. Perform RPR andTreponema pallidumparticle agglutination (TPPA) testing in the infant and mother. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that characteristic rash on the palms, soles, and scalp, along with transaminitis and hepatosplenomegaly on physical examination and ultrasound, are consistent with congenital syphilis. Topical corticosteroids (choice A) are not appropriate treatment for undiagnosed rash in an infant. Skin biopsy (choice B) is invasive and not the preferred initial option. Transaminitis and hepatomegaly with rash are not characteristic of superficial fungal infection, so KOH preparation (choice D) is not indicated. Congenital syphilis, caused by the spirocheteT pallidum,is transmitted to the fetus through the placenta or through direct contact with lesions during delivery.1Cases of congenital syphilis in the US exceeded 3800 in 2023, a more than 10-fold increase over the prior decade.2Risk factors for congenital syphilis include inadequate prenatal care, younger maternal age, lower educational attainment, low family income, unstable housing, substance use disorder, and history of incarceration.3The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends screening all pregnant women for syphilis at their first prenatal visit and in the third trimester, with risk-based screening at the time of delivery. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends universal testing 3 times in pregnancy.4-6All pregnant patients who test positive for syphilis should be treated immediately to decrease the risk of congenital syphilis.5,6 Approximately 55% of neonates with congenital syphilis are asymptomatic at birth; 31% of symptomatic cases are diagnosed after age 3 months.7Infants with early congenital syphilis (onset before age 2 years) may have bullous or mucocutaneous eruptions (40%), hepatobiliary dysfunction (33%-100%), anemia and thrombocytopenia (37%), and osteochondritis or periostitis on skeletal radiography (75%).8The classic skin rash (oval, copper-red macular or papular, often desquamating, lesions on the palms and soles or elsewhere on the body) is contagious due to presence of spirochetes in the lesions.9Up to 60% of symptomatic newborns develop neurosyphilis, which may present with seizures and/or cranial nerve palsies.8Approximately 40% of infants born to pregnant patients with untreated syphilis develop late congenital syphilis (onset after age 2 years), which may present with bony abnormalities (osteochondritis or periostitis), Hutchinson teeth (notched, widely spaced teeth), ocular abnormalities (interstitial keratitis, uveitis, chorioretinitis), and sensorineural hearing loss.8,9 The CDC stratifies patients with possible congenital syphilis into 4 categories: confirmed or highly probable, possible, less likely, and unlikely based on characteristic clinical findings and nontreponemal test results.5Because maternal nontreponemal antibodies passively cross the placenta, diagnosis of early congenital syphilis requires nontreponemal testing (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory [VDRL] or RPR) of the infant and mother, using the same assay. An infant titer of 4 or greater times the maternal titer confirms congenital syphilis.8,9Infants with physical findings (eg, characteristic rash) or an RPR titer more than 4-fold higher than the maternal titer should undergo testing with complete blood cell count, liver function tests, lumbar puncture and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, and long-bone radiographs.5 The differential diagnosis of congenital syphilis includes impetigo, fungal infection, neonatal lupus erythematosus, and SCORTCH infections (syphilis, cytomegalovirus, other viruses [eg, HIV, hepatitis B, Zika, parvovirus, rubella, toxoplasmosis, chickenpox, herpes simplex]).10 For confirmed or highly probable cases of congenital syphilis, standard therapy consists of a 10-day course of intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G.5After treatment, neonates with congenital syphilis should undergo regular monitoring of symptoms and serologic testing every 3 months until their titers decline at least 4-fold from the peak titer.9 The infant’s RPR was reactive, with a titer of 1:2048 (8-fold higher than maternal RPR [1:256]). The infant’s TPPA test result was positive. Results of HIV testing of the infant and mother were negative. Skeletal radiographs showed metaphyseal destruction on the medial aspects of the bilateral proximal tibias (Figure 2). CSF analysis showed a leukocyte count of 23 cells/μL (reference, 0-20 cells/μL), protein level of 170.9 mg/dL (reference, 15-45 mg/dL), and a reactive VDRL (titer 1:8), consistent with neurosyphilis. Findings on cerebral ultrasound, ocular examination, and hearing assessment were normal. The patient received 50 000 IU/kg of aqueous crystalline penicillin G every 6 hours for 10 days. At 6-week follow up, the infant’s skin lesions had resolved, liver function test results normalized, and the bony radiographic abnormalities had resolved. No clinical sequelae such as hearing loss, visual disturbances, or developmental delays were observed. At 9-month follow-up, the infant’s RPR titer had decreased more than 4-fold, to 1:16.

case_info.explanation: C. Perform RPR andTreponema pallidumparticle agglutination (TPPA) testing in the infant and mother. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that characteristic rash on the palms, soles, and scalp, along with transaminitis and hepatosplenomegaly on physical examination and ultrasound, are consistent with congenital syphilis. Topical corticosteroids (choice A) are not appropriate treatment for undiagnosed rash in an infant. Skin biopsy (choice B) is invasive and not the preferred initial option. Transaminitis and hepatomegaly with rash are not characteristic of superficial fungal infection, so KOH preparation (choice D) is not indicated. Congenital syphilis, caused by the spirocheteT pallidum,is transmitted to the fetus through the placenta or through direct contact with lesions during delivery.1Cases of congenital syphilis in the US exceeded 3800 in 2023, a more than 10-fold increase over the prior decade.2Risk factors for congenital syphilis include inadequate prenatal care, younger maternal age, lower educational attainment, low family income, unstable housing, substance use disorder, and history of incarceration.3The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends screening all pregnant women for syphilis at their first prenatal visit and in the third trimester, with risk-based screening at the time of delivery. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends universal testing 3 times in pregnancy.4-6All pregnant patients who test positive for syphilis should be treated immediately to decrease the risk of congenital syphilis.5,6 Approximately 55% of neonates with congenital syphilis are asymptomatic at birth; 31% of symptomatic cases are diagnosed after age 3 months.7Infants with early congenital syphilis (onset before age 2 years) may have bullous or mucocutaneous eruptions (40%), hepatobiliary dysfunction (33%-100%), anemia and thrombocytopenia (37%), and osteochondritis or periostitis on skeletal radiography (75%).8The classic skin rash (oval, copper-red macular or papular, often desquamating, lesions on the palms and soles or elsewhere on the body) is contagious due to presence of spirochetes in the lesions.9Up to 60% of symptomatic newborns develop neurosyphilis, which may present with seizures and/or cranial nerve palsies.8Approximately 40% of infants born to pregnant patients with untreated syphilis develop late congenital syphilis (onset after age 2 years), which may present with bony abnormalities (osteochondritis or periostitis), Hutchinson teeth (notched, widely spaced teeth), ocular abnormalities (interstitial keratitis, uveitis, chorioretinitis), and sensorineural hearing loss.8,9 The CDC stratifies patients with possible congenital syphilis into 4 categories: confirmed or highly probable, possible, less likely, and unlikely based on characteristic clinical findings and nontreponemal test results.5Because maternal nontreponemal antibodies passively cross the placenta, diagnosis of early congenital syphilis requires nontreponemal testing (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory [VDRL] or RPR) of the infant and mother, using the same assay. An infant titer of 4 or greater times the maternal titer confirms congenital syphilis.8,9Infants with physical findings (eg, characteristic rash) or an RPR titer more than 4-fold higher than the maternal titer should undergo testing with complete blood cell count, liver function tests, lumbar puncture and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, and long-bone radiographs.5 The differential diagnosis of congenital syphilis includes impetigo, fungal infection, neonatal lupus erythematosus, and SCORTCH infections (syphilis, cytomegalovirus, other viruses [eg, HIV, hepatitis B, Zika, parvovirus, rubella, toxoplasmosis, chickenpox, herpes simplex]).10 For confirmed or highly probable cases of congenital syphilis, standard therapy consists of a 10-day course of intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G.5After treatment, neonates with congenital syphilis should undergo regular monitoring of symptoms and serologic testing every 3 months until their titers decline at least 4-fold from the peak titer.9 The infant’s RPR was reactive, with a titer of 1:2048 (8-fold higher than maternal RPR [1:256]). The infant’s TPPA test result was positive. Results of HIV testing of the infant and mother were negative. Skeletal radiographs showed metaphyseal destruction on the medial aspects of the bilateral proximal tibias (Figure 2). CSF analysis showed a leukocyte count of 23 cells/μL (reference, 0-20 cells/μL), protein level of 170.9 mg/dL (reference, 15-45 mg/dL), and a reactive VDRL (titer 1:8), consistent with neurosyphilis. Findings on cerebral ultrasound, ocular examination, and hearing assessment were normal. The patient received 50 000 IU/kg of aqueous crystalline penicillin G every 6 hours for 10 days. At 6-week follow up, the infant’s skin lesions had resolved, liver function test results normalized, and the bony radiographic abnormalities had resolved. No clinical sequelae such as hearing loss, visual disturbances, or developmental delays were observed. At 9-month follow-up, the infant’s RPR titer had decreased more than 4-fold, to 1:16.
